Fertilised eggs of Atlantic salmon from the River Blackwater in Scotland, sourced from a 1SW mother, were incubated in the laboratory to establish baseline developmental parameters. At a constant water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], the newly emerged alevins exhibited a total length at birth of 2.825 cm [Lb = 2.825 cm]. Offspring from a separate 2SW female from the same river system provided data on initial body mass, with the wet weight at birth measuring 0.16 grams [Wwb = 0.16 grams]. This modest size at emergence is typical for the species and reflects the substantial yolk reserves that sustain the lecithotrophic alevin through the critical period before the onset of exogenous feeding. The low thermal regime significantly slows metabolic processes during embryogenesis, prolonging the developmental period compared to warmer incubation conditions. These early life-history traits are foundational for understanding subsequent growth and survival probabilities in the wild, where temperature regimes vary considerably across natal streams.

To examine the duration of embryonic development, eggs collected from a 2SW female in the River Stjordalselva, Norway, were reared under controlled conditions. The age at birth was recorded as 196 days [ab = 196 days] at an incubation temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], a relatively protracted period that underscores the retarding effect of cold water on salmonid embryogenesis. Following emergence, the yolk-sac larvae, or alevins, remain in the gravel interstitial spaces, relying on endogenous nutrition until the transition to free-swimming, exogenously feeding fry. This lengthy developmental phase is an adaptation to the cold, oligotrophic environments characteristic of many Norwegian salmon rivers, where a prolonged incubation ensures that emergence coincides with optimal spring conditions for first feeding. Comparative data from other European populations indicate that even slight increases in mean water temperature can shorten the incubation period by several weeks, highlighting the sensitivity of this early stage to thermal variation.

Data from Scottish populations provide a comprehensive picture of the species' juvenile development and life-history scheduling. Under a thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the median time since birth at metamorphosis, marking the parr-to-smolt transformation, is approximately 827 days . This profound morphological and physiological reorganisation prepares the juvenile for the marine phase of its life cycle, involving silvering, osmoregulatory changes, and a shift in behaviour. The total length at metamorphosis for these Scottish populations has a median value of 12 cm , reflecting the size threshold necessary for successful downstream migration and seawater entry. Reaching this critical size and developmental stage requires a delicate balance of growth rate and environmental conditions, and variability among individuals is considerable, influencing overall recruitment to the adult population. These metrics are essential for modelling population dynamics and assessing the impacts of climate change on juvenile survival.

The median Scottish population data also inform our understanding of sexual maturation schedules at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The time since birth at puberty is approximately 1335 days [tp = approximately 1335 days], indicating that maturation typically occurs after the smolt stage has been completed and a period of marine growth has taken place at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This relatively late age at puberty is characteristic of the species' life-history strategy, which prioritises somatic growth before reproductive investment. Historically, the maximum lifespan recorded for female Atlantic salmon comes from specimens caught in Loch Maree, Scotland, on 10th May, 1924, with a longevity of approximately 4748 days [am = approximately 4748 days], the same temperature conditions at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This exceptional age, while representing the upper extreme, demonstrates the species' potential for iteroparity under favourable conditions, although most individuals in contemporary populations exhibit far shorter life spans due to increased fishing pressure and environmental stressors.

Reproductive output in Atlantic salmon exhibits considerable variation across populations, with some of the highest rates documented for the River Almond in Scotland. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate recorded there reaches approximately 40 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 40 eggs per day], a value that underscores the species' capacity for high fecundity. In terms of adult body size, the ultimate total length for females in Scottish populations reaches a maximum of 95 cm [Li = 95 cm], representing a substantial investment in somatic growth that supports the production of large numbers of eggs. For comparative purposes, data from the Simojoki river in Finland, which drains into the Baltic Sea, indicate that the mean wet weight at metamorphosis over the periods from 1972 to 1981 and 1992 to 2004 was 25 grams . This metric provides a valuable intra-specific contrast, highlighting the influence of environmental conditions and genetic background on juvenile life-history traits across the species' geographic range.
